note: 'c. 1147 BCE' matches the uncited Wikipedia infobox ('c. 1147 BC'; text: reign of Ramesses V, 1149–1145 BCE, no citation). The hr-st transcription project README gives 'around 1160 BCE'. No named edition was opened to confirm the reign attribution. The whole-papyrus reference also needs page/line locators.

old_value: The Contendings of Horus and Seth (Papyrus Chester Beatty I)
proposed_value: The Contendings of Horus and Seth (Papyrus Chester Beatty I)
note: Identification is standard but no edition was opened: Gardiner 1931, Lichtheim AEL II and Simpson/Wente were not accessible.

old_value: the Great Ennead — psḏt (‘the Nine’)
proposed_value: the Ennead / the Great Ennead (translation); psḏt not confirmed at the passage
note: The translation uses 'the Ennead' (47 times) and 'the Great Ennead' (5 times). The Egyptian psḏt was not seen in any edition printing the text, so it is unconfirmed.

old_value: Re-Horakhty (the Lord of All)
proposed_value: The Universal Lord (sun-god), also addressed as Pre-Harakhti and Atum
note: The inspected translation says 'Universal Lord', not 'Lord of All' (Lichtheim's wording could not be checked). The same presiding god is called Pre-Harakhti and Atum. The Ennead sometimes acts against him (he asks why they exercise 'authority alone').

old_value: Thoth, Isis, Geb, Neith, Atum, Shu
proposed_value: Shu, Thoth, Onuris, Banebdjedet, Isis (litigant's mother) and the Ennead; Neith and Osiris are consulted by letter
note: Geb is not named in the story, only in the web page's glossary note on the Heliopolitan Ennead. Neith takes part only by letter, from Sais. Atum is a name of the presiding god, not a separate member.

old_value: A divine tribunal adjudicates the eighty-year succession dispute over Osiris's throne between Horus and Seth
proposed_value: A divine tribunal adjudicates the dispute between Horus and Seth over Osiris's office. The text says the case had been before the tribunal for eighty years
note: 'eighty years … in the tribunal' occurs twice: in the letter to Neith and in Horus's complaint. This makes it the length of the case, not of the dispute generally. No papyrus locator was available.

old_value: Metamorphoses 1.163–252
proposed_value: Metamorphoses 1.163–252 (flood choice 1.253–261)
note: The council runs from its summons (1.167) to Jupiter's promise of a new race (1.250–252). The flood itself is chosen just after, at 1.253–261.

old_value: concilium (deorum)
proposed_value: concilium (conciliumque vocat, 1.167); the members are called superi (1.177, 1.196)
note: Ovid writes concilium alone; 'deorum' is an editorial gloss and does not occur at the passage. More: 'he convened a council'.

old_value: Jupiter
proposed_value: Jupiter
note: He sits higher than the rest, leaning on an ivory sceptre (1.178), and silences the assembly (1.205–208).

old_value: The assembled gods — the great gods and the commoner deities
proposed_value: The superi from the noble halls of the potentes caelicolae (1.171–177). The plebs lives elsewhere (1.173), and demigods, nymphs, fauns and satyrs are spoken of as outside heaven (1.192–195)
note: The passage sets the commoner deities ('plebs habitat diversa locis') apart from the noble gods' quarter. It does not seat them in the council, so 'commoner deities' as members is not supported.

old_value: Jupiter convenes the gods, denounces Lycaon and humankind, and the assembly assents to his resolve to destroy the human race by flood
proposed_value: Jupiter convenes the gods, tells the Lycaon story and announces a sentence already sworn: the human race must perish (1.188–191, 1.240–243 'sic stat sententia'). Some gods approve aloud and others assent (1.244–245), but all grieve and ask about the future (1.246–249), and he promises a new race (1.250–252). He chooses the flood afterwards, alone (1.253–261)
note: The gods assent to destroying humankind, not to a flood. The flood is chosen after the council, in place of thunderbolts. More: 'some approved the words … others gave assent'.

old_value: Völuspá st. 6, 9, 23–25; Gylfaginning ch. 14
proposed_value: Völuspá st. 6, 9, 23, 25 (Codex Regius order; Bellows 6, 9, 24, 25); Gylfaginning ch. 14
note: The rökstóla refrain occurs in four stanzas: 6, 9, 23 and 25. Stanza 24 is the war itself. Bellows transposes MS 23/24, so his numbers are 6, 9, 24 and 25.

old_value: rökstólar (‘seats of counsel’); the regin / ginnheilög goð
proposed_value: rökstólar (acc. pl. rökstóla); regin öll; ginnheilög goð. Translations: 'assembly-seats' (Bellows), 'seats of judgment' (Brodeur)
locator: Vsp 6, 9, 23, 25 ('Þá gengu regin öll á rökstóla, ginnheilög goð, ok um þat gættusk')
note: All three terms are printed at each refrain. The gloss 'seats of counsel' is the project's own; neither inspected translator uses it.

old_value: The regin collectively; Odin in the Prose Edda
proposed_value: Völuspá: the regin collectively (no presider). Gylfaginning 14: Allfather (Odin), who set up the rulers and has the high-seat beside their twelve seats
note: Brodeur: Allfather 'established rulers, and bade them ordain fates with him … the high-seat which Allfather himself has'.

old_value: The Æsir (the ruling powers)
proposed_value: Völuspá: regin öll / ginnheilög goð. Gylfaginning 14: the rulers Allfather established (twelve seats)
note: The council stanzas say regin/goð, not æsir. St. 23 has the council debate whether the æsir should pay tribute, which implies the Vanir also have a claim to it. 'Æsir' as the members is an inference.

old_value: The gods take their seats of counsel — ordering time, resolving to fashion the dwarves, and deliberating the Æsir–Vanir war
proposed_value: The gods take the rökstólar to name night, day and the times for counting years (st. 6), to decide who should shape the dwarves (st. 9), to debate whether the æsir pay tribute or all gods share worship (st. 23), and to find who mixed the air with poison and gave Óðr's maid to the giants (st. 25). Gylf. 14: rulers ordain fates and plan the town
note: The old value leaves out st. 25 (the wall-builder / Freyja episode). St. 23 is about tribute or shared worship after the war, not the war itself.

old_value: ETCSL 1.2.1 (the Ki-ur / Ekur judgment scene)
proposed_value: ETCSL 1.2.1, lines 54–64 (Enlil seized in the Ki-ur)
note: Reference narrowed to the located passage. The scene is set in the Ki-ur (ki-ur3-ra, 54–55, 58), not 'the Ekur'. E-kur occurs only in Nuska's title, 'master builder of the E-kur' (35–53).

old_value: ukkin (the assembly) — ‘the fifty great gods’ and ‘the seven who decree the fates’ (the Anunna)
proposed_value: No assembly term in the passage. The groups are named dijir gal-gal 50-ne-ne 'the fifty great gods' and dijir nam-tar-ra 7-na-ne-ne 'the seven gods who decide destinies'
note: 'ukkin' does not occur anywhere in the ETCSL 1.2.1 composite, and neither does 'Anuna' (a-nun). Both are supplied in the baseline. The passage names the two groups but uses no assembly term.

old_value: The assembly collectively (Enlil is the defendant, not the presider)
proposed_value: None named: 'the fifty great gods and the seven gods who decide destinies' are the subjects who have Enlil arrested; Enlil is the one seized
note: The baseline's point that Enlil is not the presider holds. 'The assembly collectively' adds an institution the text does not name.

old_value: The fifty great gods; the seven Anunna who decree the fates
proposed_value: The fifty great gods; the seven gods who decide destinies
note: 'The seven Anunna' is not in the text: 7-na is the numeral seven with a suffix. Do not gloss 'the seven who decree the fates' as 'Anunna'.

old_value: The divine assembly at Nippur seizes, judges, and banishes Enlil as ritually impure for defiling Ninlil
proposed_value: In the Ki-ur, the fifty great gods and the seven who decide destinies have Enlil arrested. Enlil, 'the ritually impure' (u2-zug4), leaves the city 'in accordance with what had been decided' (2 mss.: 'Enlil, ritually impure, leave the city!')
note: 'At Nippur … judges, and banishes … for defiling Ninlil' goes beyond the text. No trial or verdict speech is narrated. The decision is reported impersonally (nij2-nam-ce3 nam mu-un-tar-ra, 61–62), and the link to the act with Ninlil is implicit from the sequence.
There is no project library book for this composition, so the empty value stands.

old_value: Adi Parva, Sections XVII–XVIII (the churning of the ocean of milk)
proposed_value: Ganguli Adi Parva Section XVII (council); XVIII (churning). Critical edition 1.15.5–13 (council), 1.16 (churning)
note: The conclave on Meru is in Section XVII alone (CE 1.15.5–13). Section XVIII is the churning, with later consultations of Vishnu and Brahmā at Mandara and mid-churning.

old_value: devasabhā / sabhā (the conclave of the celestials)
proposed_value: Sanskrit: mantrayitum ārabdhās tatrāsīnā … samāgamya ('seated there, having assembled, they began to deliberate', CE 1.15.10). Ganguli: 'held a conclave', 'the celestial assembly'
note: Neither devasabhā nor sabhā occurs in CE 1.15.5–13. The text uses mantr- (deliberate) and samāgam- (assemble). The vulgate text behind Ganguli was not inspected. 'conclave' is Ganguli's English.

old_value: Brahmā, with Nārāyaṇa (Vishnu) as counselor
proposed_value: Not stated. Nārāyaṇa speaks to Brahmā (nārāyaṇo devo brahmāṇam idam abravīt); Brahmā is the one addressed
note: No presider is named. Brahmā presides only in a rejected starred line (CE *262), where the gods and daityas approach him. Later, in Sec. XVIII, the gods come to Vishnu and Brahmā 'who were sitting'.

old_value: The devas, assembled on Mount Meru
proposed_value: All the gods (surāḥ sarve, divaukasaḥ) on the summit of Meru
note: Ganguli: 'all the mighty celestials sat them down and held a conclave'. Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa are present.

old_value: The celestials sit in conclave on Meru; Nārāyaṇa counsels Brahmā and they resolve to churn the ocean of milk for the amrita (the nectar of immortality)
proposed_value: The gods, having come for amṛta, deliberate on Meru. Nārāyaṇa tells Brahmā that gods and asuras should churn the ocean (kalaśodadhi), which will yield amṛta with all herbs and gems
note: The text has Nārāyaṇa's advice but no explicit resolution by the gods. The churning starts in the next section. The asuras' part in the churning, given in the advice, is left out of the old value.
